text: Roam the streets of Jerusalem, look and see; search her squares. If you can find one person, if there is even one who does justice and seeks faithfulness, then I will forgive her.

versions.text: Roam the streets of Jerusalem, look and see; search her squares. If you can find one person, one who does justice and seeks truth, then I will forgive her.
versions.explanation: אֱמוּנָה is better rendered "faithfulness" than "truth" here; the doubled conditional (אִם...אִם) is also flattened. The suggestion restores both while keeping the oral rhythm.

text: Even when they say, "As the LORD lives," they are swearing falsely.

O LORD, do your eyes not look for faithfulness? You struck them, but they felt no pain; you consumed them, but they refused to take correction. They set their faces harder than rock; they refused to turn back.

versions.text: O LORD, do your eyes not look for truth? You struck them, but they felt no pain; you crushed them, but they refused correction. They set their faces harder than rock; they refused to turn back.
versions.explanation: לֶאֱמוּנָה should match "faithfulness" (cf. v.1); כִּלִּיתָם means "you made an end of / consumed them" rather than "crushed."

text: So I thought, "These are only the poor; they are foolish, for they do not know the way of the LORD, the justice of their God.
Let me go to the great ones and speak with them, for they know the way of the LORD, the justice of their God." But they, one and all, had broken the yoke and torn off the bonds.

versions.text: Let me go to the great ones and speak with them, for they know the way of the LORD, the justice of their God." But they too had broken the yoke, they too had torn off the bonds.
versions.explanation: יַחְדָּו means "together / all alike," not "too." The current rendering repeats "they too" twice, which both loses the sense of collective guilt and adds an emphasis not in the Hebrew.

text: Therefore a lion from the forest will strike them down, a wolf of the desert will ravage them. A leopard lies in wait by their cities; whoever ventures out will be torn to pieces. For their rebellions are many, their turnings away are countless.

versions.text: Therefore a lion from the forest will strike them down, a wolf of the desert will ravage them. A leopard lies in wait by their cities; whoever ventures out will be torn to pieces. For their rebellions are many, their betrayals beyond counting.
versions.explanation: מְשׁוּבוֹת means "backslidings, turnings away/apostasies," not "betrayals." The Hebrew עָצְמוּ means "are numerous/mighty," so "countless" is fine but the noun should be corrected.

text: Why should I forgive you? Your children have abandoned me and sworn by gods that are no gods. I fed them full, and they committed adultery; they crowded into the house of the prostitute.
They were well-fed, lusty stallions, each one neighing after his neighbor's wife.

versions.text: They are well-fed stallions, roaming free, each one neighing after his neighbor's wife.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew verb הָיוּ is past tense, matching the surrounding narrative; "roaming free" renders a disputed word (מַשְׁכִּים) that more likely means "lusty/eager at dawn," and the current rendering adds an interpretation not clearly in the text.

text: Shall I not punish them for this? declares the LORD. Shall I not avenge myself on a nation such as this?
Go up through her rows of vines and destroy, but do not finish them off. Strip away her branches, for they do not belong to the LORD.
For the house of Israel and the house of Judah have been utterly faithless to me, declares the LORD.
They have denied the LORD and said, "It is not he! No disaster will come upon us; we will never see sword or famine.

versions.text: They have denied the LORD and said, "He is nothing. No disaster will come upon us; we will never see sword or famine.
versions.explanation: לֹא־הוּא denies that the LORD is the one behind the prophesied judgment ("It is not he" / "He will do nothing"), rather than asserting that God is non-existent. "He is nothing" risks reading a metaphysical denial into the people's words.

text: The prophets are only wind, and the word is not in them. So let it be done to them!"

versions.text: The prophets are only wind, and the word is not in them. Let what they say be done to them!"
versions.explanation: "Let what they say be done to them" adds "what they say," which is not in the Hebrew (כֹּה יֵעָשֶׂה לָהֶם = "thus let it be done to them").

text: Therefore this is what the LORD, the God of hosts, says: Because you have spoken these words, I am making my words in your mouth a fire, and this people the wood it consumes.

Listen, house of Israel: I am bringing a nation against you from far away, declares the LORD—an enduring nation, an ancient nation, a nation whose language you do not know and whose speech you cannot understand.
Their quiver is an open grave; all of them are warriors.

They will devour your harvest and your bread; they will devour your sons and your daughters; they will devour your flocks and herds; they will devour your vines and fig trees. With the sword they will batter down your fortified cities in which you trust.

versions.text: They will devour your harvest and your bread; they will devour your sons and your daughters; they will devour your flocks and herds; they will devour your vines and fig trees. With the sword they will batter down the fortified cities in which you trust.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew has the second-person suffix (מִבְצָרֶיךָ, "your fortified cities"), matching the chain of "your" possessives throughout the verse; dropping it weakens the personal address.

text: Yet even in those days, declares the LORD, I will not make an end of you.

And when they ask, "Why has the LORD our God done all this to us?" you are to tell them, "Just as you abandoned me and served foreign gods in your own land, so you will serve strangers in a land that is not yours."
Announce this in the house of Jacob, proclaim it in Judah:
Hear this, you foolish people, without understanding—you have eyes but do not see, ears but do not hear.

Do you not fear me? declares the LORD. Do you not tremble before me? I set the sand as a boundary for the sea, an everlasting limit it cannot cross. The waves rage, but they cannot prevail; they roar, but they cannot pass it.
But this people has a stubborn and rebellious heart; they have turned aside and gone their own way.
They do not say in their hearts, "Let us fear the LORD our God, who gives the rains in their season, the autumn rain and the spring rain, who keeps for us the appointed weeks of harvest."
Your wrongdoings have turned these away; your sins have withheld the good from you.

versions.text: Your wrongdoing has turned these away; your sins have withheld the good from you.
versions.explanation: עֲוֺנוֹתֵיכֶם is plural with a plural verb (הִטּוּ), and it parallels the plural "your sins" in the second half; the singular flattens the parallelism.

text: For among my people are wicked men. They lie in wait like fowlers crouching; they set a deadly snare, and it is people they catch.

versions.text: For among my people are wicked men. They lie in wait like bird-catchers crouching; they set their deadly traps and it is people they catch.
versions.explanation: מַשְׁחִית is singular ("a destroying trap/snare"); "deadly snare" reads better and matches the fowler imagery.

text: Like a cage full of birds, so their houses are full of deceit. That is why they have grown great and rich;

versions.text: Like a cage full of birds, their houses are full of what they have gained by fraud. So they have grown great and rich;
versions.explanation: מְלֵאִים מִרְמָה is simply "full of deceit"; "what they have gained by fraud" is an interpretive expansion that lengthens the line and blunts the parallel with the birds in the cage. Restoring the correlative "so" (כֵּן) also preserves the simile's rhythm for oral reading.

text: they are fat and sleek. They even overflow with deeds of evil; they do not defend the cause of the fatherless, yet they prosper, and they do not uphold the rights of the needy.

versions.text: they are fat and sleek. They overlook every evil; they will not defend the cause of the orphan, so that it prospers, and they refuse justice to the needy.
versions.explanation: עָבְרוּ דִבְרֵי־רָע means they "overflow/exceed in evil deeds," not that they "overlook" evil. Also וְיַצְלִיחוּ refers to the wicked prospering, not the orphan's cause prospering.

versions.text: they are fat and sleek. They overflow with deeds of evil; they do not defend the cause of the fatherless, yet they prosper, and they do not uphold the rights of the needy.
versions.explanation: The emphatic particle גַּם ("even, indeed") is left untranslated; adding "even" preserves the intensifying force of the clause without disturbing the previously corrected sense of עָבְרוּ דִבְרֵי־רָע.

versions.text: they are fat and sleek. They even overflow with deeds of evil;
versions.explanation: More than half of the Hebrew verse is missing from the current text. The clauses דִּין לֹא־דָנוּ דִּין יָתוֹם וְיַצְלִיחוּ ("they do not judge the cause, the cause of the fatherless, yet they prosper") and וּמִשְׁפַּט אֶבְיוֹנִים לֹא שָׁפָטוּ ("and they do not judge the case of the needy") have been dropped. The restored wording follows the previously approved rendering, keeping the correction that it is the wicked, not the orphan's cause, that prospers.

text: Shall I not punish them for this? declares the LORD. Shall I not avenge myself on a nation such as this?
An appalling and horrifying thing has happened in the land:

versions.text: Something appalling and horrible has happened in the land:
versions.explanation: "Something appalling and horrible" is vaguer and less weighty than the Hebrew pair שַׁמָּה וְשַׁעֲרוּרָה; a concrete noun phrase reads more forcefully aloud and matches the prophetic tone.

text: the prophets prophesy lies, the priests rule by their own authority, and my people love it so. But what will you do in the end of it all?

versions.text: the prophets prophesy lies, the priests rule at their side, and my people love it so. But what will you do when the end comes?
versions.explanation: עַל־יְדֵיהֶם most likely means the priests rule "by their own authority" or "at their direction," and לְאַחֲרִיתָהּ refers to the outcome/end of this state of affairs.
